explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David prays, "Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have relieved my distress…" (Psalm 4:1). He asks God to answer, and he also remembers that God relieved his distress. I think remembering what God has done is a smart way to pray.

Good guess, because David does talk about people against him later. But in verse 1 he says, "You have relieved my distress…" (Psalm 4:1). Nothing there about silencing anybody. The psalm sticks to the distress being relieved.

Friend, I can see why you'd pick it, since relief and healing sound like cousins. But the psalm says, "You have relieved my distress…" (Psalm 4:1). Sickness never comes up in these verses. David's looking back at God relieving his distress.
Yep. Right after the reminder, David asks, "show me grace and hear my prayer." (Psalm 4:1). He asks for two things, grace and a hearing. Short and sweet, no extra frosting.
This one's true, friend. The verse says, "show me grace and hear my prayer." (Psalm 4:1). David asks for grace, and he asks God to hear him. Both are right there in the first verse.
Careful, baker, that one flips it around. David says, "How long will you love vanity and seek after lies?" (Psalm 4:2). So the text says vanity and lies, not truth. The answer is False.
Right, it's False. David asks, "How long will you love vanity and seek after lies?" (Psalm 4:2). The verse names vanity and lies, not truth. So the statement doesn't match what the text says.
That's it. The psalm says, "Know that the LORD has set apart the godly for Himself…" (Psalm 4:3). The godly belong to Him in a special way. That's a good thing to know on a rough day.

explanations.answer: Made them rulers of the land
explanations.explanation: I get the pull of a crown, baker, but that's not in this verse. It says, "Know that the LORD has set apart the godly for Himself…" (Psalm 4:3). Nobody gets handed a throne here. They get set apart for Him.

explanations.answer: Sent them out to the nations
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but this verse isn't about sending anybody anywhere. It says, "Know that the LORD has set apart the godly for Himself…" (Psalm 4:3). The focus is on them being set apart for Him.
Yes, "hears." David says, "the LORD hears when I call to Him." (Psalm 4:3). That lines up with his first line, where he asks God to hear his prayer. He asks, and then he says it with confidence.
Close, but not what David says. The verse reads, "the LORD hears when I call to Him." (Psalm 4:3). The word is "hears," and it matches how David started the psalm, asking God to hear his prayer.
That's a fair guess, baker, but it's not the word. David says, "the LORD hears when I call to Him." (Psalm 4:3). He's sure that when he calls, God hears.

explanations.answer: Be angry yet do not sin
explanations.explanation: That's the line: "Be angry, yet do not sin…" (Psalm 4:4). It doesn't say anger is the problem. The command is about what you do with it. Honestly, friend, that's a tall order.

explanations.answer: Do not be angry at all
explanations.explanation: It sounds tidy, but that's not what the psalm says. It says, "Be angry, yet do not sin…" (Psalm 4:4). The warning is about sinning, not about feeling angry. Big difference, friend.
Forgiving is a good thing, baker, but it isn't in this verse. The psalm says, "Be angry, yet do not sin…" (Psalm 4:4). The command is to not sin while you're angry.
Right. The verse says, "Offer the sacrifices of the righteous and trust in the LORD." (Psalm 4:5). The two commands sit side by side. Trusting in the LORD is the second one.

Seven days, friend? With no cookies, I'd be a crumb by day two. The verse says, "Offer the sacrifices of the righteous and trust in the LORD." (Psalm 4:5). Fasting isn't mentioned there. The second command is to trust in the LORD.

Good thought, baker, but Jerusalem isn't mentioned in this psalm. The verse says, "Offer the sacrifices of the righteous and trust in the LORD." (Psalm 4:5). The second command is to trust in the LORD.

That's right, baker. Many ask, "Who can show us the good?" and David answers with a prayer: "Shine the light of Your face upon us, O LORD." (Psalm 4:6). Notice where he turns. His prayer goes straight to the LORD.

I see why you'd go there, baker, but the psalm doesn't mention priests. After many ask their question, David says, "Shine the light of Your face upon us, O LORD." (Psalm 4:6). He prays to the LORD Himself.
Good thought, friend, but no prophets show up in these verses. David says, "Shine the light of Your face upon us, O LORD." (Psalm 4:6). His prayer goes to the LORD.

Yep, and look at the size of that. David says, "You have filled my heart with more joy than when grain and new wine abound." (Psalm 4:7). He compares his joy to a time when grain and new wine abound, and says God gave him more. I can't even picture it, and I've seen a full cookie rack.

It's actually True, baker. The verse says, "You have filled my heart with more joy than when grain and new wine abound." (Psalm 4:7). The word is "more." God filled his heart with more joy than when grain and new wine abound.

explanations.answer: The LORD alone keeps him safe
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. David says, "I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety." (Psalm 4:8). The word "alone" points to the LORD as the One who makes him dwell in safety.

explanations.answer: His enemies have all gone home
explanations.explanation: That would help a person sleep, friend, but the psalm doesn't say it. David says, "…for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety." (Psalm 4:8). His safety comes from the LORD.

explanations.answer: His guards are watching the door
explanations.explanation: Nice and practical, baker, but no guards appear in this psalm. David says, "…for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety." (Psalm 4:8). The reason is the LORD, and the word "alone" says it all.
